answer.location_description: Small 3x3 square near the top-left corner of the image, rows 1-3 and columns 1-3, well away from the central blob.
answer.mechanism: Many first-layer units carry very large weights confined to the 3x3 patch at rows 1-3, cols 1-3. The 'large-blob' units (0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 10, 18, 20, 29) have strong positive patch weights, roughly +40 to +99. They feed the layer-2 units u3, u10, u12 and u13, which have positive output weights (+67, +74, +41, +38). The 'small-blob/background' units (5, 6, 9, 14, 15, 21, 24, 27, 30) have strong negative patch weights, roughly -30 to -98, so a bright patch switches them off. Those units feed u0, u1, u6 and u9, which have strongly negative output weights (-99, -90, -93, -77). A bright patch in that corner therefore drives the logit toward class 1 (large blob) through both pathways.
answer.evidence: Patch weights are far larger than any other weights in the same units. Unit 4 has 93, 98, 98, 94 in rows 1-3, cols 1-3. Unit 20 has 81-94, unit 1 has 59-98, unit 10 has 46-99. Unit 5 has -57 to -98, unit 14 has -44 to -98, unit 27 has -44 to -83. The neighbouring pixels (row 0, row 4, col 0, col 4) are near zero or of the opposite sign, so the patch has sharp edges. The sign of the patch weights in each unit matches that unit's blob role (positive with a positive central disk/ring, negative with a negative ring), so the patch acts as an additional 'large' signal. Pure-noise units such as 3, 7, 11 and 12 have no patch structure.
answer.main_feature: Genuine size cue: units respond to brightness in a broad ring/disk around the centre (roughly rows 5-17, cols 5-18). Large-blob units weight that annulus positively, while small-blob units weight it negatively and are positive on the far background, so blob extent determines the logit.
